subject: Banking
title: Dodd-Frank: The Big Reform
description: A micro-lesson that makes Dodd-Frank: The Big Reform usable.

hook.text: Dodd-Frank created 400 new rules for banks after the 2008 crash.

buildup.text: The law created the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, required stress tests.

discovery.text: The Volcker Rule banned proprietary trading — banks could no longer bet their own money on risky trades.

twist.text: Banks spent $1.5 billion lobbying against Dodd-Frank. By 2018, many provisions were weakened.

climax.text: Dodd-Frank was the response to the worst crisis since 1929.

punchline.text: 400 new rules after 2008. $1.5 billion in lobbying undid many within a decade.

quiz.question: What happened to many Dodd-Frank provisions?
options: Banks spent $1.5 billion lobbying to weaken them within a decade

details.summary: The Dodd-Frank Act of 2010 was the most sweeping US financial regulation since the 1930s, imposing stress tests, higher capital requirements, and the Volcker Rule to prevent another 2008-style financial crisis.
details.whyItMatters: Dodd-Frank reshaped American banking by limiting risky behavior and creating new oversight agencies. Its ongoing political battles reveal the tension between financial stability and industry profitability.
takeaways: It created the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau
The Volcker Rule restricted banks from proprietary trading
Annual stress tests force banks to prove crisis resilience

faq.question: Has Dodd-Frank prevented another financial crisis?
faq.answer: Banks hold significantly more capital and face stricter oversight since 2010. However, parts of Dodd-Frank were rolled back in 2018, and the 2023 regional bank failures showed that gaps in regulation remain.

faq.question: What is the Volcker Rule?
faq.answer: Named after former Fed Chair Paul Volcker, it prohibits banks from making speculative investments with depositor funds. The rule aims to prevent banks from gambling with customer money while enjoying government deposit insurance.
